section.heading: 6.4 The Gram–Schmidt Process
section.paragraph: The Gram–Schmidt process is a simple algorithm for producing an orthogonal or orthonormal basis for any nonzero subspace of $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ . The first two examples of the process are aimed at hand calculation.

example.heading: Example 1

Construct an orthogonal basis $$\left\{ \mathbf{v}_{1} \text{,} \mathbf{v}_{2} \right\}$$ for $$W$$ .

section.paragraph: The next example fully illustrates the Gram–Schmidt process. Study it carefully.

example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: Let $$\textbf{x}_{1} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\textbf{x}_{2} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 0 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , and $$\textbf{x}_{3} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . Then $$\left\{ \textbf{x}_{1} \text{,} \textbf{x}_{2} \text{,} \textbf{x}_{3} \right\}$$ is clearly linearly independent and thus is a basis for a subspace $$W$$ of $${\mathbb{R}}^{4}$$ . Construct an orthogonal basis for $$W$$ .

section.heading: Proof﻿
section.paragraph: For $$1 \leq k \leq p$$ , let $$W_{k} = \text{Span} \left\{ \textbf{x}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{x}_{k} \right\}$$ . Set $$\mathbf{v}_{1} = \textbf{x}_{1}$$ , so that $$\text{Span} \left\{ \mathbf{v}_{1} \right\} = \text{Span} \left\{ \textbf{x}_{1} \right\}$$ . Suppose, for some $$k < p$$ , we have constructed $$\mathbf{v}_{1}$$ , $$\ldots$$ , $$\mathbf{v}_{k}$$ so that $$\left\{ \mathbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{v}_{k} \right\}$$ is an orthogonal basis for $$W_{k}$$ . Define

By the Orthogonal Decomposition Theorem, $$\mathbf{v}_{k + 1}$$ is orthogonal to $$W_{k}$$ . Note that $$\text{proj} _{W_{k}}\textbf{x}_{k + 1}$$ is in $$W_{k}$$ and hence also in $$W_{k + 1}$$ . Since $$\textbf{x}_{k + 1}$$ is in $$W_{k + 1}$$ , so is $$\mathbf{v}_{k + 1}$$ (because $$W_{k + 1}$$ is a subspace and is closed under subtraction). Furthermore, $$\mathbf{v}_{k + 1} \neq \textbf{0}$$ because $$\textbf{x}_{k + 1}$$ is not in $$W_{k} = \text{Span} \left\{ \textbf{x}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{x}_{k} \right\}$$ . Hence $$\left\{ \mathbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{v}_{k + 1} \right\}$$ is an orthogonal set of nonzero vectors in the $$(k + 1)$$ -dimensional space $$W_{k + 1}$$ . By the Basis Theorem in Section 4.5, this set is an orthogonal basis for $$W_{k + 1}$$ . Hence $$W_{k + 1} = \text{Span} \left\{ \mathbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{v}_{k + 1} \right\}$$ . When $$k + 1 = p$$ , the process stops.

Theorem 11 shows that any nonzero subspace $$W$$ of $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ has an orthogonal basis, because an ordinary basis $$\left\{ \textbf{x}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{x}_{p} \right\}$$ is always available (by Theorem 12 in Section 4.5), and the Gram–Schmidt process depends only on the existence of orthogonal projections onto subspaces of $$W$$ that already have orthogonal bases.
section.heading: Orthonormal Bases
section.paragraph: An orthonormal basis is constructed easily from an orthogonal basis $$\left\{ \mathbf{v}_{1} \text{,} \ldots \text{,} \mathbf{v}_{p} \right\}$$ : simply normalize (i.e., “scale”) all the $$\mathbf{v}_{k}$$ . When working problems by hand, this is easier than normalizing each $$\mathbf{v}_{k}$$ as soon as it is found (because it avoids unnecessary writing of square roots).
section.heading: QR Factorization of Matrices
section.paragraph: If an $$m \times n$$ matrix $$A$$ has linearly independent columns $$\textbf{x}_{1}$$ , $$\ldots$$ , $$\textbf{x}_{n}$$ , then applying the Gram–Schmidt process (with normalizations) to $$\textbf{x}_{1}$$ , $$\ldots$$ , $$\textbf{x}_{n}$$ amounts to factoring $$A$$ , as described in the next theorem. This factorization is widely used in computer algorithms for various computations, such as solving equations (discussed in Section 6.5) and finding eigenvalues (mentioned in the exercises for Section 5.2).

note.title: ﻿﻿Theorem ﻿12
note.heading: ﻿﻿Theorem ﻿12
The QR Factorization﻿
note.paragraph: If $$A$$ is an $$m \times n$$ matrix with linearly independent columns, then $$A$$ can be factored as $$A = QR$$ , where $$Q$$ is an $$m \times n$$ matrix whose columns form an orthonormal basis for $$\text{Col} A$$ and $$R$$ is an $$n \times n$$ upper triangular invertible matrix with positive entries on its diagonal.

list.item: When the Gram–Schmidt process is run on a computer, roundoff error can build up as the vectors $$\mathbf{u}_{k}$$ are calculated, one by one. For $$j$$ and $$k$$ large but unequal, the inner products $$\mathbf{u}_{j}^{T}\mathbf{u}_{k}$$ may not be sufficiently close to zero. This loss of orthogonality can be reduced substantially by rearranging the order of the calculations.1 However, a different computer-based QR factorization is usually preferred to this modified Gram–Schmidt method because it yields a more accurate orthonormal basis, even though the factorization requires about twice as much arithmetic.

To produce a QR factorization of a matrix $$A$$ , a computer program usually left-multiplies $$A$$ by a sequence of orthogonal matrices until $$A$$ is transformed into an upper triangular matrix. This construction is analogous to the left-multiplication by elementary matrices that produces an $$LU$$ factorization of $$A$$ .

Construct an orthonormal basis for $$W$$ .
